summary: The production change does what M4.8b1 asks and does it at both listing sites. I verified the predicate exhaustively rather than by reading it: a standalone harness over LogKeys' exact logic accepts every key the writer can produce (5,000,000 sequential keys plus 0, 1, 15, 16, Long.MAX_VALUE-1, Long.MAX_VALUE, Long.MIN_VALUE, -1, -2, at epochs 0/1/255/Long.MAX_VALUE/-1) and refuses every non-writer shape I could construct: empty digits, leading '+', uppercase hex, unpadded, 17 digits, ckpt/<hex>.ckpt, ckpt/<hex>.delta, <hex>.delta.tmp, Arabic-Indic digits (Character.digit accepts them for radix 16, and the round-trip is what closes that), leading whitespace, the bare prefix, and the substring-overlap probe that would be the StringIndexOutOfBounds case. The round-trip equality subsumes every leniency in Long.parseUnsignedLong, so there is no key CommitLog writes that recovery now drops (no I2/I3 regression), and every write path in CommitLog -- commitSubmissions, open, seal -- goes through keyFor, so the allow-list cannot be narrower than the writer. 'continue' is right at both sites and both are pinned: I mutated chainEnd's continue to break (1 test fails), applyChain's continue to return (1 test fails), and deleted both filters (4 tests fail). I3 is untouched -- the filter reads the KEY only, and anything that passes is still decoded with the failure propagating; the full 250-test sequencer suite is green including recoveryStopsOnAnEntryItCannotUnderstandRatherThanSkippingIt. On cost: no request is added or moved. LIST count and paging are byte-for-byte unchanged (startAfter still comes from the store, not from the filter), applyChain's GETs drop from one-per-key to one-per-entry, and chainEnd stays at exactly one GET, so recovery's GET count is now constant in the number of foreign keys -- the task's claim holds. The exposure that remains is the one the row already assigns elsewhere: both sites page at maxKeys=1000 counting foreign keys, so once M4.8b2 lands, recovery's LIST count grows with the checkpoint count and hence with uptime. That is pre-existing here and is M4.8c/M4.9's AC5, not a regression this diff introduces. Three minors below; none blocks.

findings.title: The round-trip equality -- the line the whole design argument rests on -- is not pinned by any test
findings.detail: sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/LogKeys.java:79. Surviving mutation, measured rather than argued: replace `return key.equals(keyFor(sequence));` with `return true;` and the entire sequencer module stays green -- 250 tests, 0 failures, including all four of ChainReplayNonDeltaKeyTest. I ran it twice, once as `return sequence >= 0 || true;` and once as a literal `return true;`. The reason is that every interloper the new tests seed is caught one step earlier, by Long.parseUnsignedLong: `ckpt/<hex>.ckpt` fails endsWith, `ckpt/<hex>.delta` and `<hex>.delta.tmp` fail the parse. So the tests pin the parse, and the parse alone is enough to make the bare-endsWith mutant die (I confirmed that one dies: aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain fails). What no test constrains is the canonicalisation the class javadoc calls the point of the whole approach -- padding, lowercase, exactly 16 digits, 'keyFor run backwards'. Failure scenario: a later edit simplifies isEntryKey to stop at the successful parse, no test notices, and the predicate silently widens to accept `<logPrefix>9.delta`, `<logPrefix>000000000000000A.delta` and `<logPrefix>+00000000000000a.delta`, each of which recovery would then GET and decode. Not blocking, and this is why: no writer in the tree produces a non-canonical key, so the weakened predicate is behaviourally identical in production today -- the loss is the guarantee, not the behaviour. A test seeding one unpadded or uppercase `.delta` key alongside the existing two interlopers would close it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later edit simplifies isEntryKey to stop at the successful parse (or otherwise drops the key.equals(keyFor(sequence)) line); the whole sequencer suite stays green -- measured, 250 tests 0 failures with the line replaced by `return true` -- and the predicate silently widens to accept `<logPrefix>9.delta`, `<logPrefix>000000000000000A.delta` and `<logPrefix>+00000000000000a.delta`, which recovery then GETs and decodes as chain entries.

findings.title: CommitLog.isEntryKey is a delegate with no caller anywhere in the tree
findings.detail: sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/CommitLog.java:118-120. `grep -rn isEntryKey --include=*.java .` returns exactly four sites: the two uses in ChainReplay (which call LogKeys directly), the definition in LogKeys, and this delegate. No production code and no test calls CommitLog.isEntryKey. The scope-control argument that justifies keeping the keyFor/logPrefix delegates -- ten existing test files call them and a rename would ripple -- does not apply to a method this commit invents: it has no incumbent callers to protect. So it is new production surface with no caller and no test, added under a task whose scope is the filter at the two listing sites. Failure scenario is not behavioural; it is that the next reader of CommitLog reasonably takes it for a supported entry point and builds on a method no test constrains. Deleting the three lines costs nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change needs a key-ownership test and reaches for CommitLog.isEntryKey, taking it for a supported entry point; it is a method with no caller and no test, so a defect introduced in the delegation (or in a later edit to it) is caught by nothing, while the LogKeys copy that everything actually calls stays green.

findings.title: The LogKeys seam is applied at two of the three reader sites, and two comments now overstate it
findings.detail: LogKeys' javadoc says the split exists because honouring the addressing seam 'had made both readers construct a whole CommitLog, a WRITER, to ask a naming question. Naming is not writing.' ChainReplay.java:270 still does exactly that: `String slotZero = new CommitLog(store, prefix, chainEpoch).keyFor(0);` in firstEntry, on the ancestry-walk path reached by both replay() and firstInheritableAncestor(). Relatedly, ChainReplay's class javadoc at line 29 still reads 'ADDRESSING COMES FROM CommitLog, never re-derived here', which is now true of one site and stale for the other two. Second, smaller half of the same finding: swapping `new CommitLog(store, prefix, epoch)` for `new LogKeys(prefix, epoch)` at chainEnd and applyChain silently drops the constructor's guards -- CommitLog rejects a negative epoch and null-checks prefix, LogKeys (a bare record) checks nothing, and String.format does not throw on a null prefix, it formats the literal 'null'. A negative epoch would now format unsigned as ffffffffffffffff and sort AFTER every real epoch, the opposite of what CommitLog's own comment on that guard predicts. I traced every route in and it is unreachable today -- recover/recoverChainEnd come through CommitLog's validating constructor, inherited() guards prevEpoch >= 1, and every Hop epoch is >= 0 -- which is why this is minor and not major. Failure scenario for both halves is the same shape: the next reader added to ChainReplay copies whichever pattern it happens to land next to.
findings.failure_scenario: The next reader added to ChainReplay copies firstEntry's `new CommitLog(store, prefix, chainEpoch).keyFor(0)` -- a reader constructing a writer to ask a naming question -- because the class javadoc at line 29 still names CommitLog as the source of addressing, and the seam this commit created is then a second pattern rather than the pattern. Its second half: a future caller reaching ChainReplay.chainEnd or applyChain with a negative epoch or a null prefix now gets a silent wrong prefix -- ffffffffffffffff, which sorts AFTER every real epoch, or the literal string 'null' -- where the CommitLog construction it replaced threw IllegalArgumentException or NullPointerException. Unreachable through today's callers, all of which I traced.
